title: Introduction to cancer hallmarks and their genetic basis
why: The lecturer frames the session's learning outcomes and introduces the Hanahan and Weinberg hallmarks of cancer framework.

title: Mutations in extracellular signaling pathways controlling growth and survival
why: The lecturer explains how mutations in Wnt/beta-catenin, RTK/Ras/MAPK, PI3K/Akt, and TGF-beta cascades enable growth signal independence and resistance to inhibitory signals.

title: APC and β-catenin mutations in Wnt-driven proliferation
why: It explains the normal mechanism of the Wnt degradation complex and how mutations in APC and beta-catenin drive proliferation.

title: Deregulation of MAPK, PI3K–AKT and TGF-β signaling
why: It details how receptor tyrosine kinases signal through Ras-MAPK and PI3K-AKT cascades and how activating mutations promote cancer cell proliferation and survival.

title: Differentiation blocks and cell origins in hematological cancers
why: The lecturer examines how cancer cells fail to terminally differentiate, using examples from hematopoiesis, leukemias, and intestinal crypts.

title: APC loss disrupts intestinal epithelial differentiation and renewal
why: The lecturer examines differentiation failure in a solid tissue context, detailing normal crypt-villus differentiation dynamics and how APC/Wnt mutations disrupt this process.

title: Resistance to apoptosis through p53 loss and BCL2 activity
why: The lecturer details the apoptotic pathway governed by p53, MDM2, Bax pore formation, and anti-apoptotic BCL2 balance.

title: Telomere shortening, replicative limits and cellular senescence
why: The lecturer describes the Hayflick limit, telomere shortening, TERT activation mechanisms, and stress-induced senescence.

title: TERT promoter mutations and rearrangements enabling immortalization
why: The lecturer moves from the normal telomere biology and senescence barrier to the specific oncogenic mutations (promoter point mutations and rearrangements) that reactivate telomerase in cancer cells.

title: p53-mediated stress responses preserve genome integrity
why: The lecturer explains how p53 integrates multiple stress signals—telomere shortening, DNA damage, and oncogene activation—to safeguard genome integrity through arrest, senescence, or apoptosis.

title: Summary of growth control hallmarks and introduction to broader cancer behaviors
why: The lecturer takes stock of the genetic mutation-driven hallmarks of growth control covered so far and previews the upcoming set of hallmarks.

title: The Warburg effect and glucose uptake in cancer diagnosis
why: The lecturer explains aerobic glycolysis, diagnostic PET imaging, and Krebs cycle mutations producing oncometabolites that alter the epigenome.

title: Cancer metabolic rewiring retains tissue-specific features
why: The lecturer moves from the specific mechanism and reasons behind the Warburg effect to discussing a study on broad metabolic rewiring across diverse cancer types and tissues of origin.

title: Oncometabolites and feedback between metabolism and the epigenome
why: It examines whether metabolic alterations are causes or effects of cancer by detailing Krebs cycle enzyme mutations and the resulting oncometabolites and epigenetic changes.

title: The angiogenic switch in tumor development and growth
why: The lecturer explains the angiogenic switch, oxygen diffusion limits, timing during pre-malignant stages, and the balance of activators and inhibitors.

title: Metastatic dissemination, circulatory routes and clinical monitoring
why: The lecturer discusses the metastatic cascade, lymph node mapping, circulating tumor cells as liquid biopsies, seed-and-soil compatibility, and whole genome duplication.

title: Metastatic inefficiency and seed–soil compatibility
why: The lecturer explains why metastatic colonization is highly inefficient and how successful metastasis depends on mechanical factors and the compatibility between cancer cells and the target tissue environment.

title: Shared driver mutations and whole-genome duplication in metastases
why: The lecturer examines sequencing studies comparing primary and metastatic tumors, explaining that metastases are clonal derivatives lacking specific driver mutations but often exhibiting whole genome duplication.

title: Lecture summary: diverse genetic routes converge on cancer hallmarks
why: The lecturer concludes the session with overarching remarks on the hallmarks framework and points to recommended reading.
